title: A World Lit by Flames
summary: Long ago, when the Sun went down, the world went dark. People lit their homes with fires, smoky candles, smelly whale-oil lamps and flickering gas jets. Every light was a tiny fire, and every fire could be dangerous.

sections.heading: When the Sun Went Down
paragraphs: Imagine it is a winter evening in a farming village in England about three hundred years ago. It is only five o'clock, but the Sun has already slipped behind the hills. There are no streetlights. There is no glow from the next town on the horizon. Unless the Moon is up, the lane outside your door is so dark that you cannot see your own hand. If you need to cross the yard to check on the animals, you carry a lantern with a single candle inside it, and the circle of light it makes is about the size of a kitchen table.

Indoors, the brightest thing in the room is the fire in the hearth. Your family sits close to it, partly for warmth and partly because it is the only place where you can see well enough to mend a sock or whittle a stick. Your mother might light one candle for the evening, but candles cost money, so she will blow it out the moment the work is done. Reading a book at night is a luxury. Most people simply went to bed early, and in the darkest months of the year that could mean a very long night indeed.

For almost all of human history, this was normal. The day was for working and the night was for sleeping, because there was very little else you could do in the dark. Farmers, fishers and travellers planned their lives around the Moon. A full Moon meant you could walk home safely after a market or a wedding. A new Moon meant you stayed in. Towns had night watchmen who walked the streets calling out the hour, and in many cities people who went out after dark were expected to carry their own light.

Darkness was not just inconvenient. It was dangerous. People tripped down stairs, fell into ditches and rivers, and were robbed in unlit alleys. And the only way to fight the dark was to set something on fire. Every candle, every lamp and every torch was a small, open flame, sitting in houses built of wood, thatch and cloth. When a candle was knocked over in the night, a whole street could burn.

In this first part of our story we will meet all the different flames people used to push back the night, from Ice Age lamps burning animal fat to the gas lights and kerosene lamps of the 1800s. Each one was a little better than the last. But each one was still fire. Keep that in mind, because the real hero of this Deep Dive is a strange, invisible force that could one day make light with no flame at all.

sections.heading: Fire, Fat and the First Lamps
paragraphs: The very first artificial light was the campfire. Our ancestors were using fire tens of thousands of years ago, and probably much longer. A fire gave warmth, cooked food, scared away animals and let a group of people see each other's faces after sunset. A burning branch pulled from the fire became the first torch, a light you could carry.

Torches have a problem, though. They burn quickly, drip, spark and smoke, and they are hard to use inside a cave or hut without filling it with fumes. So people invented something cleverer: the lamp. A lamp is simply a container that holds fuel, usually fat or oil, with a wick that soaks up the fuel and burns slowly at its tip. Instead of burning a whole stick at once, you burn a little bit of fuel at a time.

Archaeologists have found curved stone lamps from more than ten thousand years ago. One famous example was discovered in 1940 at Lascaux in France, the cave whose walls are covered in paintings of horses, deer and bulls. Ice Age artists needed light to paint deep underground, and hollowed-out stones filled with animal fat, with a wick of moss or plant fibre, gave them a steady, smoky glow. Picture an artist kneeling in the cold, the lamp spluttering beside them, painting a galloping horse by a light about as bright as a birthday candle.

Some archaeologists think people also used seashells as lamps more than six thousand years ago. A shell makes a perfect little bowl for oil. In the ancient Sumerian cities of what is now Iraq, people even carved lamps out of alabaster stone in the shape of shells, around 2600 BCE. Later, potters began making lamps of baked clay. The earliest were simple round bowls with a pinched edge to hold the wick. Over the centuries they grew spouts, handles and lids.

By Roman times, clay oil lamps were everywhere. Factories in northern Italy and southern Gaul (modern France) turned them out by the thousand between the first and third centuries CE, and ships carried them all over the Roman Empire. Many were stamped with the maker's name and decorated with gods, gladiators, animals or chariot races. Museums today are full of them, because they were cheap, common and tough enough to survive in the ground for two thousand years.

What did people burn? Whatever their land provided. Around the Mediterranean it was mostly olive oil, which burns fairly cleanly. Elsewhere people used sesame, castor, flax, walnut and almond oils, or animal fuels such as butter, ghee, fish oil, seal oil and whale oil. Fish and animal oils smoked more than olive oil, which may be why some ancient lamps had several wick spouts to make up for a dimmer flame.

An ancient oil lamp gave a small, yellow, wobbling flame. It was enough to find your way to bed or eat supper by, but not enough to light a whole room brightly. Rich families might have a dozen lamps hanging from bronze stands. Poor families might have one, or none.

sections.heading: Candles: Tallow, Beeswax and Rushlights
paragraphs: Candles are a lamp with the container taken away. The fuel is a solid block of fat or wax, and the wick runs through the middle. When the wick is lit, the heat melts a little pool of fuel at the top, the wick soaks it up, and the flame burns it. A candle needs no bowl and spills no oil, which made candles easy to carry and store.

The Romans made candles by dipping a wick again and again into melted tallow or beeswax. Tallow is hard animal fat, usually from cattle or sheep. In China, candles may have been made more than two thousand years ago, possibly from whale fat. But for centuries, oil lamps stayed more common in the Mediterranean, partly because beeswax was so expensive.

In medieval Europe there were two very different kinds of candle. Beeswax candles burned with a clean, bright flame and smelled sweet. They were costly, so they were used mostly in churches and in the homes of the rich. Ordinary households burned tallow candles. Tallow was cheap because every butcher had it, but it smelled of burning meat fat, smoked badly, dripped greasy blobs and needed its wick trimmed often, or the flame would sink into a sooty, flickering stub. By the 1200s candle-making was an organised craft in England and France, with guilds of chandlers, as candle-makers were called.

The very poorest people often could not afford even tallow candles. Instead they made rushlights. In summer or autumn they gathered tall rushes from damp meadows, peeled away most of the green outer skin, and dried the white, spongy pith inside. Then they dipped it in whatever fat they had, often bacon grease saved from cooking. The result was a thin, fragile stick that was clamped in a little iron holder and lit.

A naturalist named Gilbert White, who lived in the village of Selborne in Hampshire, described rushlights in a famous letter written in 1789. He timed one that was about 72 centimetres long and found it burned for 57 minutes, giving what he called 'a good clear light'. Rushlights were still used in parts of rural Britain until the end of the 1800s. Think about that: in the same years that factories and railways were changing the world, some families were still lighting their evenings with greasy reeds.

In the 1700s and 1800s, candles got better. A waxy substance from sperm whales, called spermaceti, made hard, bright, clean-burning candles. In 1823 the French chemists Michel Eugène Chevreul and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac found how to separate a harder material called stearin from animal fat, which made firmer candles that gave a brighter light. In 1825 a braided wick was introduced that curled over and trimmed itself as it burned, so nobody had to keep snipping it. In 1834 Joseph Morgan built a machine that moulded candles quickly, and in the 1850s the Scottish chemist James Young began producing paraffin wax from coal and oil shale. Paraffin wax soon became the most common candle material, and it still is today.

The candle was so important that it became a unit of measurement. For a long time, the brightness of a lamp was described in 'candlepower', meaning how many candles it equalled. The modern scientific unit of light intensity is called the candela, the Latin word for candle, and a typical candle gives out roughly one candela. When later in this story you hear that an early electric lamp equalled sixteen candles, you will know exactly what people meant.

sections.heading: Sailing Around the World for Lamp Oil
paragraphs: In the 1700s and 1800s, one of the best lamp fuels came from the sea. Whale oil burned brighter and cleaner than most animal fats, and the oil from sperm whales was the finest of all. Light, in other words, came from one of the largest animals on Earth.

The island of Nantucket, off the coast of Massachusetts, began whaling in 1690. At first its sailors hunted whales close to shore. As those whales grew scarce, Nantucket crews sailed farther and farther, and by the 1700s whaling had become a big, deep-sea business. After the American Revolution ended in 1783 the industry recovered, and the town of New Bedford grew into the busiest whaling port of all.

Whalers especially wanted sperm whales. Inside a sperm whale's enormous head is a waxy liquid called spermaceti, which burns with a very bright flame and made the best candles money could buy. To find sperm whales, ships sailed to the far side of the planet: down around South America into the Pacific, to the waters off Peru and Ecuador, across the equator and as far as Japan. A single voyage could last years. Sailors left home as teenagers and came back as young men, if they came back at all.

Life on a whaling ship was hard and dangerous. Men rowed small wooden boats right up to a whale, threw harpoons by hand, and then had to survive the giant animal's struggle. Afterwards the crew cut up the whale and boiled its blubber in huge iron pots on deck to make oil, which was stored in barrels below. About ten thousand seamen worked on American whaling ships during the industry's busiest years, including more than three thousand African American sailors. Crews were paid not with wages but with a share, or 'lay', of the profits from the oil, so a voyage that found few whales could leave a sailor with almost nothing after years at sea.

In the mid-1800s, the 'golden age' of American whaling, whale oil lit homes, shops, lighthouses and factories, and it also oiled the machines of the Industrial Revolution. A clever new lamp helped too. In 1780 the Swiss inventor Aimé Argand designed a lamp with a hollow, tube-shaped wick and a glass chimney. Air flowed up through the middle of the wick as well as around the outside, so the oil burned more completely, with a brighter, steadier flame and much less smoke. Argand lamps quickly replaced older oil lamps in homes that could afford them.

But hunting whales for light came at a terrible cost to the whales. Population after population was hunted down, and whalers had to sail ever farther to find more. Today we know that several whale species were pushed close to extinction by centuries of hunting. In the end it was not kindness that saved the sperm whales from the lamp-oil trade. It was a cheaper fuel pumped out of the ground, which we will meet in a moment.

sections.heading: A Flame Through a Pipe: The Gas Light Revolution
paragraphs: Around 1792, in the mining town of Redruth in Cornwall, a Scottish engineer named William Murdoch tried an experiment that would change the look of cities. Murdoch worked for the famous steam-engine firm of Boulton and Watt, looking after their engines in the Cornish tin and copper mines. In his spare time he heated coal in a closed iron container, called a retort. When coal is heated without enough air to burn, it gives off a gas that can be lit. Murdoch piped this coal gas through tubes and lit it at the other end. By about 1794 he was lighting rooms of his house this way. His home in Redruth is often called the first house lit by gas.

Murdoch was not the only person playing with coal gas. A Dutch professor, Jean-Pierre Minckelers, had written about flammable gases in 1784, and one of his students later said he sometimes used gas to light his lecture room in Leuven. In France, Philippe Lebon lit his house in Paris with gas from wood in 1801. As we will see again and again in this Deep Dive, big ideas often occur to several people at once. But Murdoch was the one who turned gas lighting into a practical, working system.

In 1798 Murdoch moved back to Boulton and Watt's Soho Foundry near Birmingham and lit part of the main building with gas. In 1802, to celebrate a peace treaty between Britain and France called the Peace of Amiens, he lit up the outside of the factory for crowds to see. Then, starting in 1805, he lit an entire cotton mill in Manchester, belonging to the firm of Philips and Lee. It began with 50 gas lights and eventually had 904. Mill owners loved gas: it was brighter than candles, cheaper to run, and the workers could keep spinning cotton long after dark. In 1808 the Royal Society gave Murdoch its Rumford Medal for his work. Oddly, he never patented his gas lighting, so he never earned a fortune from it.

Lighting a single mill was one thing. Lighting a whole city meant building gasworks, digging up streets and laying pipes under them. A German-born showman and promoter named Frederick Albert Winsor set out to do just that in London. He gave dramatic demonstrations of gas light, including one at the Lyceum Theatre in 1804, and pushed for a company to supply gas through pipes. Parliament approved the plan in 1810, and on 30 April 1812 the Gas Light and Coke Company received its royal charter from King George III. It was the first company of its kind in the world, set up to make gas at a central works and pipe it to customers.

On the last night of 1813, Westminster Bridge in London was lit with gas lamps. People came out just to stare. Gas lighting spread quickly: Baltimore, in the United States, lit its first gas street lamp in February 1817, and Paris began lighting streets with gas in 1820. By 1823 many towns and cities across Britain had gasworks. A new job appeared, too: the lamplighter, who walked the streets every evening with a long pole to turn on and light each lamp, and came back at dawn to put them out.

Gas light changed how cities felt at night. Shops could stay open later. Theatres glowed. Streets felt safer. Still, gas had a dark side. The gas made from coal was poisonous to breathe, and if a pipe leaked or a tap was left open, a room could fill up and explode at the touch of a flame. Gas flames gave off heat, fumes and soot that blackened ceilings and wilted houseplants. And in theatres, where hundreds of gas jets lit the stage, fires were frighteningly common. Several hundred theatres in Europe and America burned down during the 1800s.

Late in the century, in 1891, the Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach invented the gas mantle, a little fabric net soaked in special chemicals. Heated by a gas flame, the mantle glowed a brilliant white and made gas lights several times brighter. Gas lamps would fight back against electric light for years thanks to this invention. Some cities, including parts of London, still keep a few gas streetlamps burning today for their old-fashioned charm.

sections.heading: Rock Oil and the Kerosene Revolution
paragraphs: Gas lighting needed pipes, and pipes only made sense in towns. Out in the countryside, on farms and in small villages, people still depended on candles and oil lamps. What they needed was a cheap liquid fuel that burned brightly. They found it underground.

In 1846 a Canadian scientist named Abraham Gesner is reported to have shown off a lamp fuel he distilled from bitumen, a black, tar-like mineral. He later named it kerosene. It was meant to be a cheaper substitute for whale oil. In 1853, in the city of Lemberg (now Lviv in Ukraine), a Polish pharmacist named Ignacy Łukasiewicz made kerosene from petroleum, the black 'rock oil' that seeped out of the ground in some places, and built a lamp to burn it. His lamp is often called the first modern kerosene lamp. In Britain the same fuel came to be called paraffin.

The real explosion came in the United States. People in western Pennsylvania had long noticed oil oozing up from the ground and floating on streams. A Yale chemist, Benjamin Silliman Jr., studied this oil and reported in 1855 that it could be refined into an excellent lamp fuel. A company called the Seneca Oil Company hired a former railroad conductor, Edwin Drake, to find a way to get the oil out in large amounts. With the help of a blacksmith and well-driller named William A. Smith, Drake drilled into the ground beside Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania. On 27 August 1859, at a depth of 69.5 feet (about 21 metres), they struck oil.

Drake's well pumped up about 12 to 20 barrels a day. That does not sound like much today, but it started a rush. Within months, wooden derricks were sprouting all along Oil Creek, and the price of oil tumbled. Drake's well was not the first oil well in the world, but it showed that drilling could provide a steady, large supply, and it launched the American oil industry. Almost all of that early oil was refined into kerosene for lamps. Petrol for cars was, at first, a nearly useless leftover.

A kerosene lamp works like this. The fuel sits in a glass or metal bowl at the bottom. A flat cloth wick dips into it, and the kerosene creeps up the wick by capillary action, the same way water creeps up a paper towel. A small knob raises or lowers the wick to make the flame bigger or smaller. A tall glass chimney around the flame creates an upward draught that pulls in fresh air, so the fuel burns more completely and brightly. Because kerosene is thin and runny, the fuel tank could sit below the flame, which made the lamps simple and cheap.

Cheap is the key word. Kerosene lamps brought decent light to millions of homes that had never been able to afford much more than a candle or two. Families could read, sew, study and talk in the evening. From the time of the American Civil War onward, kerosene steadily pushed whale oil out of the market, and the great whaling fleets shrank. Kerosene lamps are still used today in places without electricity, in parts of Africa and Asia, though the World Health Organization warns that their fumes are harmful to breathe.

sections.heading: Smoke, Soot and the Price of Light
paragraphs: By the 1870s, a well-off family in London, Paris or New York had more ways to light their home than ever before: gas jets on the walls, kerosene lamps on the tables and candles for carrying upstairs. Yet every one of these lights had the same basic problems, because every one of them was a fire.

First, flames were dim. A kerosene lamp gives somewhere between about 8 and 100 lumens, depending on its size. A lumen is a measure of how much light something gives out. A single ordinary household LED bulb today gives around 800 lumens, the light of dozens of candles, from something that stays cool enough to touch. A Victorian reading lamp would seem gloomy to us.

Second, flames were dirty. Candles and lamps gave off smoke and soot that blackened ceilings, curtains and paintings and had to be scrubbed off. Glass chimneys needed cleaning every day. Wicks needed trimming. Gas and kerosene left a smell in the air, and burning anything uses up oxygen and fills a closed room with stuffy, unhealthy fumes. Many people also blamed hours of reading by flickering flames for headaches and tired eyes.

Third, flames were dangerous. A lamp knocked off a table, a candle left by a curtain or a child's sleeve brushing a flame could start a deadly fire. Kerosene that had been mixed with more explosive fuels could flare up. Gas leaks could cause explosions. Theatres, mills and crowded homes all knew the terror of fire spreading from a single light.

And fourth, light was expensive. This is easy to forget. Economists Roger Fouquet and Peter Pearson studied seven hundred years of lighting in Britain, adding up the cost of fuel, the cost of the lamps and how efficiently they turned fuel into light. Their work shows that the price of a fixed amount of light has fallen enormously, so that today the same amount of light costs only a tiny fraction of what it did in 1800. Another economist, William Nordhaus, made a similar point in the 1990s, showing that ordinary price statistics hugely underestimate how much cheaper light has become. For a working family in the early 1800s, even a couple of candles each evening was a real expense, which is why so many simply went to bed when it got dark.

Meanwhile, scientists had been studying a very different kind of energy for over two hundred years. They knew how to make it spark and crackle. They had stored it in jars, drawn it down from thunderclouds, and made it flow through wires. By the 1870s a few dazzling electric arc lamps were even lighting streets and lighthouses. But nobody yet had a way to use electricity to light an ordinary living room safely, softly and cheaply. That challenge, and the people who solved it, is what this Deep Dive is all about.

So here is the big question. Every light in human history, from the Lascaux lamp to Murdoch's gas jets, had been a fire. What if light could come without any flame at all? The answer, strangely enough, began with a piece of rubbed amber, thousands of years ago.

deepDive: How much better was each new light? Scientists compare lamps by luminous efficacy: lumens of light produced for each watt of power used. A candle releases roughly 80 watts of heat but only about 13 lumens of light, an efficacy of well under 1 lumen per watt. Oil and kerosene lamps did somewhat better, and Welsbach's 1891 gas mantle was a big jump because the glowing mantle turned more of the flame's heat into visible light. Early carbon-filament electric bulbs managed only a few lumens per watt, and later tungsten bulbs about 12 to 15, yet they were still far cleaner and safer than flames. Modern LEDs often exceed 100 lumens per watt. So, measured in light per unit of energy, lighting has improved by a factor of hundreds. Economic historians argue about how to measure what this meant for people. In a famous 1996 study, William Nordhaus pointed out that standard price indexes track the cost of goods like candles and lamp oil, not the cost of the light itself, and so they miss most of the improvement. Roger Fouquet and Peter Pearson rebuilt the British record back to 1300, combining fuel prices, equipment costs and efficiency. Their data show light becoming dramatically cheaper over the 1800s and 1900s while people used vastly more of it: as light got cheaper, people did not simply save money, they bought far more light. Economists call this kind of effect a rebound. Historians also debate the credit for gas lighting. Minckelers is said to have lit his lecture room with gas in the 1780s, Lebon demonstrated gas in Paris in 1801, and Murdoch lit his Cornish house in the early 1790s; Murdoch's achievement was turning the idea into reliable industrial systems, while promoters such as Winsor created the business model of gas piped from a central works. That pattern, with many inventors and a few system-builders, will appear again with the electric light.
funFact: The scientific unit of light intensity, the candela, is named after the candle, and an ordinary candle gives out roughly one candela.

check.q: Who lit his house in Redruth, Cornwall with coal gas in the 1790s?
